title: Reading query plans
summary: SCAN, SEARCH, COVERING INDEX, TEMP B-TREE: what the plan is telling you, and what to do about it.

steps.title: The words in a plan
body: SQLite's plans use a small vocabulary:
```text
SCAN rides                                         every row of the table
SEARCH rides USING INDEX rides_rider (rider_id=?)  index lookup, then fetch each row
SEARCH rides USING COVERING INDEX rides_rider (rider_id=?)
everything needed is in the index:
the table is never touched
SEARCH s USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)       lookup by primary key
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY                       sort the results afterwards
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY                       sort to group
AUTOMATIC COVERING INDEX                           SQLite built a temporary index for
this one query: you probably want a real one
Joins show one line per table, in the order they're visited. The **first** table is the outer loop; for each of its rows, the next table is searched.

setup: CREATE TABLE stations (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, district TEXT NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 40) INSERT INTO stations SELECT i, 'Station ' || i, CASE i % 4 WHEN 0 THEN 'Docklands' WHEN 1 THEN 'Old Town' WHEN 2 THEN 'Northside' ELSE 'Harbourside' END FROM n;

CREATE TABLE rides (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, rider_id INTEGER NOT NULL, station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES stations(id), started TEXT NOT NULL, minutes INTEGER NOT NULL, fare_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 20000) INSERT INTO rides SELECT i, (i * 7919) % 500 + 1, (i * 31) % 40 + 1, datetime('2026-01-01', '+' || ((i * 7) % 300) || ' days', '+' || ((i * 13) % 1440) || ' minutes'), (i * 37) % 55 + 2, ((i * 37) % 55 + 2) * 15 FROM n;
CREATE INDEX rides_rider ON rides (rider_id);
sqlplan.query: SELECT id, started, minutes FROM rides WHERE rider_id = 42 ORDER BY started
index: CREATE INDEX rides_rider_started ON rides (rider_id, started);
sqlplan.note: With `started` as the second key, the matching index entries are already in date order, so the extra sort step disappears.

steps.prompt: With an index on `rides (rider_id)`, this plan has two lines. Which change removes the second line?
code: SELECT * FROM rides WHERE rider_id = 42 ORDER BY started;
-- USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
steps.explain: In an index on (rider_id, started), rider 42's entries are already sorted by started, so no separate sort is needed.

steps.title: Kill the sort
prompt: SELECT id, started, minutes FROM rides WHERE rider_id = 42 ORDER BY started;

and the plan shows `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY`. Replace the existing index **`rides_rider`** with an index named **`rides_rider_started`** on **`rides (rider_id, started)`**, so the rows come out of the index already sorted. (An index on (rider_id, started) serves lookups by rider_id alone too, so the old one becomes redundant.)

Tables: `stations(id, name, district)` (40 rows) and `rides(id, rider_id, station_id, started, minutes, fare_cents)` (20,000 rows; `started` is text like `'2026-03-14 08:05:00'`).; the index `rides_rider` on `rides (rider_id)` exists.
solution: CREATE INDEX rides_rider_started ON rides (rider_id, started);

steps.title: Joins in the plan
body: ```sql
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT r.id, s.name
FROM rides AS r JOIN stations AS s ON s.id = r.station_id
WHERE r.rider_id = 42;
```text
SEARCH r USING INDEX rides_rider (rider_id=?)
SEARCH s USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)
Read it as a **nested loop**: find rider 42's 40 rides via the index; for each, look up its station by primary key. 40 + 40 lookups, not 20,000.

When the inner table has no usable index, you'll see `SCAN` on the inner line, which means *scan the inner table once per outer row*, or SQLite building an `AUTOMATIC COVERING INDEX` to rescue you. Both say: add an index on the join column.

setup: CREATE TABLE stations (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, district TEXT NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 40) INSERT INTO stations SELECT i, 'Station ' || i, CASE i % 4 WHEN 0 THEN 'Docklands' WHEN 1 THEN 'Old Town' WHEN 2 THEN 'Northside' ELSE 'Harbourside' END FROM n;

CREATE TABLE rides (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, rider_id INTEGER NOT NULL, station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES stations(id), started TEXT NOT NULL, minutes INTEGER NOT NULL, fare_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 20000) INSERT INTO rides SELECT i, (i * 7919) % 500 + 1, (i * 31) % 40 + 1, datetime('2026-01-01', '+' || ((i * 7) % 300) || ' days', '+' || ((i * 13) % 1440) || ' minutes'), (i * 37) % 55 + 2, ((i * 37) % 55 + 2) * 15 FROM n;
sqlplan.query: SELECT r.id, s.name FROM rides AS r JOIN stations AS s ON s.id = r.station_id WHERE r.rider_id = 42
sqlplan.note: The tree shows the nested loop: the outer line runs once, the inner line runs once per outer row. `stations` is always found by its primary key.

items: `SCAN` on a 10-million-row table in a page that shows 20 rows
`USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` on millions of rows
steps.explain: Scanning a tiny table is fine; indexes have overhead too. Plans matter on big tables and hot queries.

steps.title: Group without sorting
prompt: SELECT station_id, COUNT(*) FROM rides GROUP BY station_id;

Its plan is `SCAN rides` plus `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY`: every ride is read, then sorted into groups. Create an index named **`rides_station`** that lets SQLite read the rides **already grouped**, straight from the index. Check the new plan with the Run button.
Tables: `stations(id, name, district)` (40 rows) and `rides(id, rider_id, station_id, started, minutes, fare_cents)` (20,000 rows; `started` is text like `'2026-03-14 08:05:00'`).

Index the grouped column. The plan becomes `SCAN rides USING COVERING INDEX rides_station`.

steps.title: A query that can use the index
prompt: Using the index on `rides (rider_id)`, return rider **42**'s rides with the station name: **id**, **name** (the station's), **minutes**, sorted by **id**.
Run it with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` first to see both tables searched, then submit the query itself.
Tables: `stations(id, name, district)` (40 rows) and `rides(id, rider_id, station_id, started, minutes, fare_cents)` (20,000 rows; `started` is text like `'2026-03-14 08:05:00'`).
solution: JOIN stations AS s ON s.id = r.station_id
